meta.titre: Structure of the Earth: layers, discontinuities and the evidence for them
meta.sous_theme: Crust, mantle, core and seismic discontinuities

sections.contenu_markdown: The deepest boreholes ever drilled reach only about 12 km, a tiny fraction of the 6370 km to the centre of the Earth. Even so, we know that the planet is layered, that its centre is a ball of metal and that part of it is liquid. This knowledge comes from earthquake waves, from meteorites, from the density of the planet and from its magnetic field. At Advanced Level you are asked to describe the composition and physical properties of the crust, mantle and core, to state what each seismic discontinuity marks, and to give the evidence, so every statement needs a reason.

items: P waves travel through solids and liquids, S waves through solids only, and wave speed changes with the density and rigidity of the rock.
Density is mass divided by volume, and granite, basalt and peridotite are igneous rocks of increasing density.
Temperature and pressure both increase with depth inside the Earth.
A wave changes direction (is refracted) when its speed changes at a boundary.

sections.titre: Layers of the Earth: composition, properties and discontinuities
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Compositional layers
The Earth has a mean radius of about 6370 km and a mean density of about $5.5\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, much more than the $2.7\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ of common surface rock, so the interior must be made of much denser material.

| Layer | Depth | Composition | State | Density ($\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continental crust | surface to about 35 km (average; thicker under mountain belts) | mainly granitic (rich in silica and aluminium, felsic) | solid, brittle | about 2.7 |
| Oceanic crust | about 5 to 10 km thick | basalt and gabbro (mafic, richer in iron and magnesium) | solid, brittle | about 3.0 |
| Mantle | base of the crust to 2900 km | peridotite (ultramafic), mainly olivine and pyroxene | solid rock that flows very slowly; partly molten in the asthenosphere | about 3.3 to 5.5 |
| Outer core | 2900 km to about 5150 km | iron and nickel, with some lighter elements | liquid | roughly 10 to 12 |
| Inner core | 5150 km to the centre | iron and nickel alloy | solid, because of the very high pressure | roughly 13 |

### Physical properties and reasons
- **Crust:** the thinnest layer, cool and brittle. Continental crust is thick and light, so it stands high; oceanic crust is thin and dense, so it lies low (isostasy: the crust floats on the denser mantle).
- **Mantle:** over 80 % of the Earth's volume. It is solid, as shown by S waves passing through it, but it is so hot and under such pressure that over geological time it deforms plastically and slowly circulates by convection, which drives the plates.
- **Core:** the outer core is liquid, as shown by the absence of S waves; its movement generates the Earth's magnetic field. The inner core is solid because the pressure raises the melting point above the temperature. The core is about 16 % of the volume.

### Lithosphere and asthenosphere
The **lithosphere** is the rigid outer shell made of the crust and the uppermost mantle, about 100 km thick on average. The **asthenosphere** below it is hot, weak and partly molten, and the plates of the lithosphere move over it. These layers are defined by strength, not by composition.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you are asked what a named discontinuity marks, or how seismic evidence locates a boundary.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A **discontinuity** is a depth at which the speed of seismic waves changes abruptly because the material changes in composition or state.

| Discontinuity | Approximate depth | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| Conrad | roughly 15 to 20 km in continents, not always detected | boundary between the upper, granitic crust and the lower, more basaltic crust; a small increase in P-wave speed |
| Moho (Mohorovicic) | about 5 to 10 km under oceans, about 35 km (up to about 70 km under mountains) under continents | base of the crust; P-wave speed rises sharply to about 8 km per second as the rock changes from crust to peridotite of the mantle |
| Gutenberg | about 2900 km | mantle and outer core boundary; P-wave speed falls sharply and S waves stop, showing that the outer core is liquid |
| Lehmann | about 5150 km | outer core and inner core boundary; P-wave speed increases again, showing a solid inner core |

variantes.nom: Evidence for the structure of the Earth
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question says how do we know, or asks for direct and indirect evidence.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Direct evidence** reaches only the outer few tens of kilometres: boreholes and mines (only about 12 km deep), xenoliths (fragments of the deep crust and mantle carried up in magma, for example in basalt), volcanic eruptions and ophiolites (slices of oceanic crust and upper mantle thrust onto land).

**Indirect evidence:**
- *Seismic waves:* refraction, reflection, changes in speed, the S-wave stop at the outer core and the P-wave shadow zone locate and characterise each layer.
- *Density:* a mean density of $5.5\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ against $2.7\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ at the surface requires a dense core.
- *Meteorites:* stony meteorites resemble the mantle and iron meteorites resemble the core, and they are thought to be fragments of broken bodies formed with the Earth.
- *Magnetic field:* it is explained by the motion of a liquid, electrically conducting outer core.
- *Heat flow:* temperature rises with depth, typically by roughly 25 to 30 degrees Celsius per km in the upper crust.

sections.enonce_markdown: A seismic wave is sent vertically downward from the surface of a continental area and reflected from the base of the crust. The echo returns after 10.8 s, and the average P-wave speed in the crust is $6.5\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Take the radius of the Earth as 6370 km, the mantle and outer core boundary at 2900 km and the outer and inner core boundary at 5150 km. (a) Calculate the depth of the boundary and name it. (b) Calculate the thickness of the mantle. (c) Calculate the thickness of the outer core and the radius of the inner core. (d) Calculate the fraction of the Earth's volume occupied by the whole core.

etapes.action: Convert the two-way time to a one-way time.
etapes.justification: The wave goes down and returns, so it covers the depth twice.

etapes.action: Calculate the depth and name the boundary.
etapes.justification: Distance equals speed multiplied by time.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $d = 6.5 \times 5.4 = 35.1\ \mathrm{km}$, the Moho (base of the continental crust)

etapes.action: Calculate the thickness of the mantle.
etapes.justification: The mantle lies between the Moho and the 2900 km boundary.

etapes.action: Calculate the thickness of the outer core and the radius of the inner core.
etapes.justification: The outer core is between 2900 km and 5150 km depth; the inner core extends from 5150 km depth to the centre, so its radius is the total radius minus that depth.

etapes.action: Find the volume fraction of the core.
etapes.justification: Volume of a sphere is proportional to the cube of the radius, so the fraction is the cube of the ratio of the radii.
etapes.resultat_markdown: core radius $= 6370 - 2900 = 3470\ \mathrm{km}$; fraction $= \left(\dfrac{3470}{6370}\right)^{3} = 0.545^{3} = 0.16$, that is about 16 %

sections.conclusion_markdown: The boundary is the **Moho at 35.1 km**, the mantle is about **2865 km** thick, the outer core is **2250 km** thick, the inner core has a radius of **1220 km**, and the core fills about **16 %** of the volume of the Earth although its radius is more than half of the Earth's.

items.erreur_markdown: The mantle is a layer of liquid magma.
items.pourquoi_faux: The mantle is solid rock, as the passage of S waves shows. It flows only very slowly, and it is partly molten only locally, for example in the asthenosphere.
items.correction_markdown: The mantle is **solid** (peridotite) but deforms plastically over geological time; the liquid layer is the **outer core**.

items.erreur_markdown: The whole core of the Earth is liquid.
items.pourquoi_faux: Only the outer core is liquid. The inner core is solid because the very high pressure raises the melting point above the temperature.
items.correction_markdown: **Outer core: liquid. Inner core: solid.** Both are mainly iron and nickel.

items.erreur_markdown: The Moho is the boundary between the mantle and the core.
items.pourquoi_faux: The Moho separates the crust from the mantle. The mantle and core boundary is the Gutenberg discontinuity.
items.correction_markdown: Moho = base of the crust (about 35 km under continents). Gutenberg = mantle and core boundary (about 2900 km).

items.erreur_markdown: The crust and the lithosphere are the same thing.
items.pourquoi_faux: The lithosphere contains the crust and also the rigid uppermost part of the mantle. The crust is defined by composition; the lithosphere is defined by strength.
items.correction_markdown: Lithosphere = crust plus uppermost rigid mantle, about 100 km thick on average, resting on the weak asthenosphere.

items.erreur_markdown: Continental crust is made of basalt, like the ocean floor.
items.pourquoi_faux: Oceanic crust is basaltic and gabbroic, but continental crust is overall less dense and more silica-rich (granitic).
items.correction_markdown: **Continental crust: granitic and thicker. Oceanic crust: basaltic and thinner.**

items.enonce_markdown: Name the layer or boundary described. (a) The rock layer extending from the Moho to the Gutenberg discontinuity. (b) The liquid layer that generates the Earth's magnetic field. (c) The thinnest compositional layer. (d) The boundary at which S waves stop and P waves slow down.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The **mantle**, a solid ultramafic layer of peridotite.

(b) The **outer core**, a liquid iron-nickel layer whose motion generates the field.

(c) The **crust**, which is only about 5 to 10 km thick under oceans and about 35 km on average under continents.

(d) The **Gutenberg discontinuity** at about 2900 km, between the mantle and the outer core.

items.enonce_markdown: A vertical echo from the Moho beneath an ocean basin returns 2.2 s after the signal leaves the sea floor. The average P-wave speed in the oceanic crust is $6.5\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. (a) Calculate the thickness of the oceanic crust. (b) Compare it with a continental thickness of 35 km. (c) Explain why continental crust stands higher than oceanic crust.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) One-way time $= 2.2 \div 2 = 1.1\ \mathrm{s}$; thickness $= 6.5 \times 1.1 = 7.15\ \mathrm{km}$, about 7 km.

(b) $35 \div 7.15 = 4.9$, so the continental crust is about five times as thick.

(c) Continental crust is thicker and less dense (about $2.7\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ against about $3.0\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$). By isostasy the thick, light continental crust floats higher on the denser mantle, like a thick block of wood floating higher than a thin and denser block.

**Oceanic crust: about 7 km; the continental crust is about five times thicker and stands higher.**

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Take the radius of the Earth as 6370 km and the inner core boundary at 5150 km depth. Calculate the percentage of the Earth's volume occupied by the inner core. (b) Explain how seismic waves show that the outer core is liquid and the inner core is solid. (c) Discuss the composition and physical properties of the core, and say why the core is thought to be mainly iron.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Inner core radius $= 6370 - 5150 = 1220\ \mathrm{km}$. Fraction $= (1220 \div 6370)^3 = 0.1915^3 = 0.0070$, that is **0.70 %** of the volume (the whole core is about 16 %).

(b) S waves, which cannot cross liquid, are not recorded beyond the core on the far side of the Earth, so the outer core is liquid. P waves are refracted at the Gutenberg discontinuity, which makes a shadow zone from about 103 to 142 degrees. Within the core, the speed of P waves rises again at about 5150 km (the Lehmann discontinuity), showing a change to a solid inner core.

(c) The core is made mainly of iron with nickel and some lighter elements. Its density (about 10 to 13 $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$), the high mean density of the Earth, iron meteorites and the magnetic field all support this. The outer core is liquid and flows; the inner core is solid under immense pressure; temperatures are of several thousand degrees Celsius.

**Inner core: 0.70 % of the volume; liquid outer core, solid inner core, composition iron and nickel.**

items_markdown: Compositional layers: crust (continental granitic, about 35 km; oceanic basaltic, 5 to 10 km), mantle (peridotite, to 2900 km), liquid outer core (to about 5150 km) and solid inner core, both iron and nickel.
The Earth's mean density of about 5.5 is far above that of surface rock (about 2.7), so the interior is dense.
Discontinuities: Conrad inside the continental crust, Moho at the base of the crust, Gutenberg at the core boundary (S waves stop), Lehmann at the inner core boundary.
Lithosphere (crust plus rigid upper mantle) rests on the weak asthenosphere; the layers are defined by strength, not composition.
Evidence is mostly indirect: seismic waves, density, meteorites and the magnetic field; direct samples come from the outer few tens of kilometres at most.
